analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 23.5% of firms in health care and social assistance reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 22.0% in the prior period, making healthcare one of the more measurable sectors for tracking adoption over time. That incremental but consistent rise suggests deployment is broadening rather than spiking, which fits an industry where procurement cycles are long and clinical risk tolerance for unproven tools is low.

The infrastructure underpinning clinical AI sits largely in public research institutions. NIH's data science and AI programs fund the datasets and methods that clinical AI is built on, working across electronic health record data, omics data, imaging data, and disease-specific data with an explicit goal of making biomedical information findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable for AI and machine learning applications. NIH describes unique needs that can drive the development of novel approaches, which positions it as both a funder and a shaping force for what problems the field pursues.

Measuring whether models are actually good enough for clinical use has become its own discipline. OpenAI released HealthBench, a benchmark built in partnership with 262 physicians who have practiced in 60 countries, covering 5,000 realistic health conversations each graded against physician-written rubric criteria, with 48,562 unique rubric criteria in total. HealthBench reports that OpenAI's frontier models improved by 28% on the benchmark in recent months, and that smaller, cheaper models have improved substantially, with one small model outperforming an August 2024 flagship model despite being 25 times cheaper. The benchmark also emphasizes reliability, noting that a single unsafe or incorrect answer can outweigh the benefit of many good ones, and current worst-of-n performance curves show significant room for further gains. Artificial Analysis provides a parallel, vendor-neutral comparison of models across quality, price, output speed, and latency, offering a crosscheck on vendor claims that is independent of any single developer.

On the vendor and capital side, KLAS Research has benchmarked healthcare IT vendors on real-world provider experience since 1996, gathering feedback from executives, physicians, nurses, and administrators to rate clinical AI products against actual performance rather than marketing. Rock Health tracks the venture funding flowing into digital health and clinical AI, and its research series is the standard record of where capital is concentrating, though the specific funding figures from its most recent publications are not detailed in the excerpts available here. Together these two organizations give buyers and investors a factual basis for comparing what vendors claim against what providers report and what money is actually backing.

The governance posture is set internationally by the WHO, whose guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health is the reference document for member-state health systems. Produced after eighteen months of deliberation among experts in ethics, digital technology, law, and human rights, it establishes six consensus principles requiring that AI for health put ethics and human rights at the center of design, deployment, and use, and contains recommendations to hold both public and private stakeholders accountable to healthcare workers and affected communities. For any organization deciding whether to deploy clinical AI, the practical implication is that regulatory and ethical expectations are already codified at a global level, meaning procurement cannot treat governance as an afterthought, and that benchmarks like HealthBench and vendor ratings from KLAS offer the clearest available evidence for making defensible decisions about which tools meet the bar.
